parts.text:
7
What is the definition of acceleration?
A
change in velocity per unit time
B
rate of change of speed per unit time
C
rate of change of velocity per unit time
D
resultant force per unit mass

hints: Notice the difference between velocity and speed in the wordings, and that velocity is a vector while speed is a scalar.
Recall that rate of change already means divided by time, so check what happens when per unit time is added a second time.
Check which wording gives $\Delta v / \Delta t$ with unit $\text{m s}^{-2}$ for change in velocity per unit time.
walkthrough: Start with what acceleration describes: how the vector quantity velocity changes with time, measured in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
Write the defining equation as $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$, where $\Delta v$ is change in velocity and $\Delta t$ is time taken.
In words this is change in velocity divided by time, or change in velocity per unit time.
Reject the speed wording because speed omits direction, so turning at constant speed would wrongly give zero acceleration.

Reject the force wording because resultant force per unit mass uses $a = F/m$ and states a result of Newton's second law, not the definition, and reject rate of change per unit time because it divides by time twice.
Only change in velocity per unit time matches $\Delta v / \Delta t$ with the correct unit. This is option A

A.explanation: Matches $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$, change in vector velocity divided by time with unit $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

B.explanation: Uses speed, which is scalar, so it misses direction change that vector acceleration must include.

C.explanation: Says rate of change per unit time, but rate already means per time, so this divides by time twice and would give $\text{m s}^{-3}$.

D.explanation: Gives $a = F/m$ from $F = ma$, which is equal in value but is Newton's second law, not the kinematic definition.
